outputs.L1:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Wearing a plaid green A-line spring skirt from her new fashion line, paired with a black patent leather belt and black leather gladiator sandal stilettos, "Sex and the City" actress Kristin Davis strikes the perfect balance between sweet and fierce when we meet up after her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia.

Kristin Davis surrounded by models and Belk store official Arlene Goldstein.

It's a look that unmistakably evokes her character, Charlotte, with a touch of her screen pal Carrie. Davis so closely resembles her character—adorable and upbeat—that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to interrupt our conversation with some scandalous remark.

As any true fan knows—indeed, as every woman knows—watching "Sex and the City" was like sitting front row at a fashion show with a plot. TV show and movie costume designer Patricia Field dressed the characters in haute couture as they sashayed down the streets of New York City in $600 stilettos.

But is this reality? Most sensible women wouldn't choose to walk even a single city block in high heels. And most women certainly can't afford to spend a month's rent on a belt or handbag, even for a truly fabulous party. So what about the rest of us—the fashionistas on a budget? Are we to be overlooked, resigned to dull clothing and practical shoes?

Fortunately, no; designers are taking note. Target offers affordable lines from high-end designers like Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Every piece in Sarah Jessica Parker's clothing line, Bitten, cost less than $20, before the clothing store that carried them went under.

Davis is the latest celebrity to join the clothing label bandwagon, designing a line for Belk department stores. Will she meet the same fate as Parker? Davis certainly has the credentials to succeed. Although her character was by far the most conservatively dressed (recall Carrie strolling through town in nothing but a bra top?), she had the most wearable wardrobe, and Davis became a fashion icon alongside the rest of the ladies.

Her favorite piece from her line? "I can't decide—it's impossible to choose!" she says. So I choose for her: the gladiator heels, without question.

"It's important for women to have a strong shoe," she says. "Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you're good to go."

She admits she didn't have a defined style before meeting Field, who bluntly informed her that "Sexy Secretary" would be her look. Davis' philosophy is a sound one: stick with what works. She embraces the look that Field crafted for her "Sex and the City" character. Original it may not be, but everything gracing the runway is something the stylish Charlotte York would undoubtedly wear.

Davis remains attuned to the everyday woman, saying, "I don't want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear." Her solution? Dresses, shoes and swimsuits worthy of a "Sex and the City" episode that you don't need Park Avenue pockets to afford—versatile enough to flatter every body type.

"Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!" she says with a laugh.

Davis won't reveal any secrets from the script of the "Sex and the City" movie sequel, due out in May 2010, but she does admit it's a "happy" film. She hints that our famous foursome might have to rein in their clothing expenses a little—as art imitates life. And she's happy to share a few fashion tips: How to look as though you've just stepped out of the wardrobe room on the set of the next "Sex and the City" movie? Green. "It's THE color," she says.

And really, who doesn't need to save some green? It all works out perfectly.

I left my meeting with Davis to browse her displays, then skipped out into the streets of Atlanta in a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals—which I got on sale, of course.

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- When I sit down with "Sex and the City" star Kristin Davis following her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia, she strikes just the right balance between charming and bold. She's dressed in a green plaid A-line spring skirt from her own new clothing collection, accented with a black patent leather belt and towering black leather gladiator sandal stilettos.

Kristin Davis stands among models alongside Belk store representative Arlene Goldstein.

The ensemble screams her on-screen persona, Charlotte, with just a hint of her television friend Carrie mixed in. Davis so closely resembles the character she plays -- cheerful and endearing -- that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to burst into our chat and say something outrageous to startle her.

Every devoted fan understands -- actually, let's be honest, every woman understands -- that tuning into "Sex and the City" felt like scoring a front-row seat at a runway show complete with a storyline. Costume designer Patricia Field, who worked on both the series and the films, outfitted the characters in high fashion as they pranced through the streets of New York City wearing $600 heels.

But does any of that reflect real life? Hardly any level-headed woman would voluntarily hoof it down a single city block in stilettos. And the vast majority of women simply cannot drop an entire month's rent on a belt or handbag -- no matter how glamorous the occasion calling for it.

So where does that leave the rest of us, the style lovers who have to watch our wallets? Are we destined to be overlooked and stuck in dull outfits and sensible footwear? Thankfully, no -- the designers are figuring it out. Target now carries budget-friendly collections from luxury names such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. And every single item in Sarah Jessica Parker's Bitten line was priced under $20, at least until the retailer selling them shut down.

Now Davis joins the growing list of stars launching their own labels, creating a collection for Belk department stores. Could she wind up sharing Parker's outcome? Davis has what it takes to make it work. Even though her character dressed far more modestly than the others (remember Carrie parading around in nothing but a bra top?), Charlotte sported the most practical, real-world wardrobe, and Davis rose to fashion-icon status right alongside her co-stars.

Which item from her line does she love best? "I can't decide, impossible to choose!" she tells me. So I'll settle it for her: it has to be the gladiator heels. "It's important for women to have a strong shoe," she explains. "Then you can wear anything on top. With a strong shoe on, you're good to go."

She confesses that she lacked a clear sense of personal style until she crossed paths with Field, who flatly informed her that "Sexy Secretary" would be her signature look. Davis embraces a smart approach: lean into what works. She's borrowing the aesthetic that Field crafted for her "Sex and the City" role. It may not break new ground, but every piece that glides down the runway is something the fashion-forward Charlotte York would absolutely wear.

Davis clearly relates to ordinary women, noting, "I don't want to make clothing that only skinny actresses could wear." Her answer? Dresses, shoes and swimwear straight out of a "Sex and the City" scene that don't require Park Avenue-level bank accounts. The pieces are flexible enough to flatter any figure. "Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all of my family members trying on the outfits!" she says, laughing.

Davis stays tight-lipped about the plot of the "Sex and the City" movie sequel, set for release in May 2010, though she reveals it's an upbeat film. She does drop a hint that our beloved quartet may need to rein in their wardrobe spending, mirroring real-world realities. And she's happy to pass along a few style pointers: Want to look like you just walked off the set of the upcoming "Sex and the City" film? Go green. "It's THE color," she says. And really, who couldn't use holding onto a little more green?

Everything comes together nicely. After wrapping up my conversation with Davis, I wandered over to browse her displays. Then I bounded out onto the streets of Atlanta wearing a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals -- ones I snagged on sale, naturally.

"Sex and the City" actress Kristin Davis, much like her upbeat and endearing character Charlotte York, has launched her own affordable fashion line, now available at Belk department stores. This new venture allows Davis to translate her on-screen style sensibilities into wardrobe pieces that everyday women can actually incorporate into their lives.

The move addresses a longstanding disconnect between television fashion and reality. While "Sex and the City" famously showcased haute couture and expensive designer items throughout its run, such extravagant fashion remains unrealistic and unaffordable for most women. The glamorous outfits worn by the show's characters, though aspirational, often carried price tags far beyond what the average viewer could justify spending.

Davis's line reflects a broader industry trend, as fashion designers increasingly cater to budget-conscious shoppers. Major retailers like Target have led the way in this movement, offering affordable collections from high-end designers such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. These collaborations have proven that stylish, designer-inspired clothing need not come with a prohibitive cost, opening the door for accessible fashion to reach a wider audience.

Davis is not the first "Sex and the City" star to explore this territory. Her former co-star Sarah Jessica Parker previously launched a low-cost clothing line called Bitten, in which every piece was priced under $20. Despite the appeal of its affordability, the store carrying the line eventually went out of business, illustrating the challenges that can accompany even well-intentioned fashion ventures.

Nevertheless, Davis appears well-positioned for success. Throughout the series, her character Charlotte was known for having the most wearable and realistic wardrobe among the main cast. Charlotte's classic, elegant, and approachable style helped establish Davis as a genuine fashion icon—one whose taste aligns naturally with the practical needs and preferences of everyday shoppers. This authentic connection between the actress and her signature aesthetic may prove to be the key ingredient that sets her new fashion line apart.

# From Park Avenue Princess to Peachtree Style: Kristin Davis Brings Accessible Fashion to Atlanta

*The "Sex and the City" star talks Charlotte, affordability, and dressing real women at her Belk launch*

**ATLANTA** — There's a particular kind of energy that fills a department store when a genuine star walks the floor, and on a warm Saturday afternoon at Belk's flagship location, that energy is palpable. Racks of carefully curated dresses, blouses, and accessories line the space, and at the center of it all stands Kristin Davis—poised, gracious, and looking every bit like the woman who spent six seasons teaching America how to accessorize with heart.

But this isn't Manhattan. And Davis, best known as the impeccably dressed Charlotte York on HBO's cultural juggernaut "Sex and the City," is quick to point out that's exactly the point.

"Charlotte would have loved a good deal, honestly," Davis says with a laugh, settling into a chair surrounded by pieces from her new collection. "People forget that beneath all that polish, she was practical. She cared about looking put-together, but she also cared about *value*."

## The Charlotte Connection

For millions of women, Charlotte York represented a certain aspirational elegance—the tailored coats, the pearls, the effortlessly feminine silhouettes that defined a New York state of mind. Yet Davis is careful to separate the fantasy of the character's Upper East Side lifestyle from the reality most women live.

"When I played Charlotte, we were dressing for a world where a single blouse might cost more than someone's rent," Davis reflects. "And I love those clothes—I do. But over the years, women would come up to me and say, 'I love that look, but I could never afford it.' That stayed with me."

That sentiment became the seed of her Atlanta venture: a fashion line built around the radical idea that timeless style shouldn't require a designer budget.

## Fashion Democracy at Belk

Partnering with Belk—the Southern retail institution with deep roots across Georgia and beyond—Davis has crafted a collection that emphasizes versatility, comfort, and price points that don't require a second thought at checkout.

"I wanted every piece here to work for a real woman's real life," she explains, gesturing toward a wrap dress in deep emerald. "The mom rushing between school pickup and a work meeting. The nurse who wants to feel beautiful when she goes out. The college student building her first professional wardrobe. This is for them."

The pieces reflect that philosophy. There are mix-and-match separates designed to stretch across a week's worth of outfits, dresses that transition from office to evening, and accessories that add a touch of Charlotte-worthy sophistication without the sticker shock.

## Why Atlanta?

The choice of Atlanta as a launch city wasn't accidental. The metro area has become a thriving hub for fashion, film, and Southern retail culture—a place where style feels both aspirational and grounded.

"There's something so genuine about the women here," Davis says. "They know who they are. They have a strong sense of self, and they dress with intention. Atlanta felt like the right place to say, 'This is fashion for everyone.'"

Shoppers who lined up early seemed to agree. Among them was Denise Carter, a longtime "Sex and the City" fan who drove in from Marietta.

"Charlotte was always my favorite," Carter admitted, holding a blouse she planned to buy. "But honestly, I came because it's actually affordable. That means more to me now than the celebrity part."

## A New Chapter

As the afternoon wound down and the crowd thinned, Davis remained warm and unhurried, posing for photos and chatting with shoppers about everything from hemlines to the enduring legacy of the show that made her a household name.

Asked what she hopes women take away from her line, she doesn't hesitate.

"Confidence," she says simply. "I want a woman to put on one of these pieces, look in the mirror, and feel like the best version of herself—without having emptied her wallet to get there. That's the real luxury."

Charlotte York would surely approve.

*Kristin Davis's collection is available at Belk locations and online.*

# The Charlotte in All of Us

## Kristin Davis on Style, Substance, and Whether *Sex and the City* Fashion Can Actually Fit Into Real Life

*By [Staff Writer]*

There's a particular kind of magic that happens when you sit across from someone who spent years embodying one of television's most beloved style icons. Kristin Davis—forever linked in our cultural memory to the impeccably put-together Charlotte York—settles into her chair with an easy warmth that immediately dismantles any expectation of untouchable glamour.

"People always assume I walked around in couture," she laughs, wrapping her hands around a mug of tea. "The truth is, most of us were freezing on set in gorgeous clothes that were pinned within an inch of their lives."

It's a fitting entry point for a conversation I've been wanting to have for years: In an era when nearly every celebrity has a clothing line, and when *Sex and the City* fashion continues to influence trends decades after it first aired, can the average woman actually achieve that iconic look? Or is it, like so much of Hollywood, beautiful fiction?

### The Fantasy and the Price Tag

Let's be honest about the elephant in the room. The wardrobe that made Carrie, Charlotte, Miranda, and Samantha legends was assembled with resources most of us will never have—stylists, unlimited budgets, and access to designer archives.

"That show was a fantasy," Davis acknowledges. "The apartments, the shoes, the fact that a freelance writer could afford Manolos—we all knew it wasn't realistic. But I don't think that's why people loved it. They loved what the clothes *represented*. Confidence. Joy. The idea that getting dressed could be an act of self-expression rather than obligation."

This distinction matters as we navigate the modern celebrity fashion landscape. From Rihanna's Fenty empire to Victoria Beckham's ready-to-wear line, famous names have flooded the market with clothing that promises to bring a piece of their world into ours. Some deliver genuine value; others trade on nostalgia and name recognition alone.

### What Celebrity Lines Get Right—and Wrong

The best celebrity clothing lines, Davis suggests, understand something crucial: authenticity can't be manufactured.

"When someone genuinely cares about design, you can tell," she says. "The pieces have a point of view. When it's just a licensing deal with a name slapped on it? That falls apart in the wash—sometimes literally."

She's not wrong. Industry watchers have long noted the gulf between celebrity lines that reflect real involvement and creative vision versus those that function as pure merchandising. The former can offer accessible entry points into aspirational style; the latter often disappoint at exactly the moment the fantasy meets the fitting room.

### Charlotte's Enduring Lesson

If any *Sex and the City* character offered a genuinely attainable style blueprint, it might have been Charlotte—the woman whose polished, classic sensibility relied less on shock value and more on timeless principles.

"Charlotte's whole thing was elegance and intentionality," Davis reflects. "That's actually the most achievable style of all, because it's not about the label. It's about fit, about caring, about presenting yourself with a little bit of thought. You can find that at any price point."

This is perhaps the most useful takeaway for real women hoping to capture some of that television magic. The secret was never the four-figure handbag. It was the *approach*—treating personal style as a form of storytelling, a daily opportunity to communicate who you are.

### So, Is It Achievable?

By the end of our conversation, Davis has reframed my entire question.

"Ask yourself what you're really chasing," she says. "If it's the exact outfit, no—you'll drive yourself crazy and broke. But if what you loved was how those women *felt* in their clothes? That's completely yours to have. You don't need our budget. You just need to decide that getting dressed matters."

It's a democratic vision of style, one that cuts through the aspirational marketing of celebrity clothing empires to arrive somewhere more honest. The women of *Sex and the City* weren't compelling because of their price tags. They were compelling because they used fashion to move through the world with intention.

And that, unlike a pair of vintage Manolos, is something every one of us can afford.

# Kristin Davis Launches Affordable Fashion Line, Talks Real Bodies and Teases 'Sex and the City' Sequel

*The actress opens up about designing accessible fashion and drops hints about the highly anticipated second film*

Kristin Davis is stepping out from behind her iconic role as Charlotte York and into the fashion spotlight with the launch of her new affordable clothing collection—one she says is designed with everyday women in mind.

The "Sex and the City" star unveiled her line this week, emphasizing that stylish, quality pieces shouldn't come with a designer price tag.

## Fashion for the Real World

"I wanted to create something that women could actually afford and actually wear," Davis said. "Not everyone can drop thousands on a single dress, and they shouldn't have to in order to feel beautiful."

The collection focuses on versatile, flattering pieces intended to work across a range of body types—a priority Davis says was non-negotiable throughout the design process.

"So much of fashion is designed for one type of figure, and that's just not reality," she explained. "I designed these clothes for real bodies—for curves, for different heights, for women who want to feel confident whether they're a size 2 or a size 16. That mattered to me more than anything."

Davis added that her years on "Sex and the City," a show celebrated for its bold fashion moments, gave her a unique perspective. "I've been so lucky to wear incredible clothes on the show, but I always thought about the women watching who wanted that feeling for themselves. This line is a little bit of that magic, made accessible."

## Teasing the 2010 Sequel

Of course, no conversation with Davis would be complete without questions about the upcoming "Sex and the City" sequel, set to hit theaters in 2010. The actress couldn't hide her excitement, even as she kept details close to the vest.

"I can't say too much, but I will tell you the fans are going to be very happy," Davis teased with a laugh. "The four of us are back together, and there's a real energy to this one. It feels bigger."

When pressed about her character's storyline, Davis stayed coy. "Charlotte's journey continues in ways I think people will love. That's all I can say!"

The first "Sex and the City" film was a box office success in 2008, and anticipation for the follow-up is running high among the show's devoted fan base.

## Looking Ahead

For now, Davis says she's thrilled to juggle both her acting career and her new entrepreneurial venture. "I get to do what I love and hopefully help women feel great about themselves. That's a pretty wonderful place to be."

# When Carrie Comes to Charlotte: Belk's Runway Proves High Fashion Doesn't Require High Prices

*On the ground at Belk's fall preview, where designer dreams meet department-store reality*

---

The lights dim inside the Belk showroom, and for a moment, the crowd of buyers, bloggers, and local fashion devotees falls silent. Then the music swells—a pulsing, cosmopolitan beat that could have scored any Manhattan sidewalk strut—and the first model emerges in a swirl of jewel-toned silk and confidence.

It's hard not to think of Carrie Bradshaw.

Nearly two decades after *Sex and the City* first taught a generation that fashion could be a form of self-expression bordering on religion, the show's influence still radiates through moments like this one. The DNA is unmistakable: the fearless mixing of high and low, the reverence for a killer heel, the belief that what you wear announces who you are before you say a word.

## The Gospel According to Carrie

Let's be honest about what *SATC* actually gave us. Beyond the cocktails and the callback-worthy one-liners, it delivered a philosophy: style is democratic in ambition, if not always in price tag. Carrie paired thrift-store finds with Manolos. She wore a nameplate necklace and a tutu with equal conviction. The message wasn't "spend more"—it was "commit harder."

That commitment is exactly what's on display at Belk today.

## The Runway Report

The fall collection leans into what I'd call "accessible aspiration." A camel coat with architectural shoulders opens the show—the kind of piece that photographs like a four-figure investment but retails for a fraction. Models glide past in wrap dresses that nod to Diane von Furstenberg's enduring formula, in wide-leg trousers cut with surprising precision, in sequined tops built for a Charlotte girl's night that could hold their own in any borough.

The real revelation, though, is in the details. A structured handbag here. A statement earring there. These are the accessories that do the heavy lifting of transformation—the great equalizers of the fashion world.

## In Defense of the Heel

And then there are the shoes.

A parade of heels crosses the runway—block heels, kitten heels, a few brave stilettos—and the audience visibly leans forward. There's a reason *SATC* made footwear into character development. A heel changes your posture, your stride, your entire relationship to a room. It's transformation you can literally step into.

Belk's offerings understand the modern truth Carrie herself would eventually learn: the most beautiful shoe means nothing if you can't survive the night in it. The standout is a two-inch block heel in oxblood suede—elegant, walkable, and priced like something you could actually justify buying two of.

## The Celebrity Designer Democracy

The most compelling story on the rack, however, is the rise of the celebrity-fronted, budget-friendly design line. Once dismissed as vanity projects, these collections have matured into something genuinely useful—giving shoppers a curated point of view at a price point that doesn't require a Charlotte-sized savings account.

The best of them deliver on the original *SATC* promise: that good taste shouldn't be gatekept behind a designer boutique's glass door. When a celebrity name attaches to a $60 blazer that's cut like a $600 one, the result is exactly the kind of high-low alchemy Carrie built a career—and a shoe collection—around.

## The Takeaway

As the final model completes her turn and the lights come up, the applause carries a note of genuine enthusiasm. What Belk offers isn't a fantasy of unlimited spending. It's something more practical and, honestly, more inspiring: the tools to build a wardrobe with intention.

Carrie Bradshaw once said she liked her money right where she could see it—hanging in her closet. The gift of shows like this one is that you can have that closet without the credit card debt.

Turns out you don't need a Manhattan salary to walk like you own the sidewalk. You just need the right pair of shoes—and the confidence to wear them like they cost twice as much.

# The Woman Who Made Me Question Every Dollar in My Closet

*In which our reporter meets a fashion visionary and learns that looking expensive is, ironically, about paying attention—not paying up.*

---

The first thing you notice about Kristin Davis is that she has clearly never met a room she couldn't own.

I find her backstage at the Atlanta Convention Center, twenty minutes after her show has wrapped, in that peculiar postshow atmosphere where the adrenaline hasn't quite decided whether to keep the party going or collapse into a heap. She's leaning against a folding table like it's a marble mantelpiece, a plastic cup of prosecco in one hand, and she is—I want to be precise about this—wearing the kind of outfit that makes you immediately audit your own.

"You're staring at the blazer," she says before I've introduced myself. "Everyone stares at the blazer."

I was, in fact, staring at the blazer. It's a structured ivory number with shoulders that mean business, paired with wide-leg trousers the color of strong espresso and a silk camisole that catches the light like it's being paid to. On her feet: pointed slingbacks in a shade of nude so precise it seems to have been engineered in a lab. She looks, in a word, expensive.

"Guess how much," she challenges, extending a hand for me to shake.

I hazard a number. It's a big number. I feel confident about the number.

She laughs—a genuine, delighted cackle that turns two nearby assistants' heads. "You're off by about eighty percent, honey."

---

## The Gospel According to Kristin

This is Davis's entire thing, it turns out. Her show, cheekily titled *"Rich on Purpose,"* was a ninety-minute argument against the idea that style has a price tag. The runway featured looks assembled from a chaotic mix of consignment finds, department-store basics, and exactly three genuinely pricey statement pieces used across the entire collection.

"People think luxury is a receipt," she tells me, waving her prosecco for emphasis. "It's not. Luxury is *fit*. It's *posture*. It's knowing that a nineteen-dollar white tee, if it hits your collarbone right, will read richer than a designer sweatshirt hanging off you like a tarp."

She says this with the conviction of a woman who has clearly won several arguments about it.

I ask about the blazer. The famous blazer. The one that fooled me.

"Thrift store in Decatur," she says, savoring it. "Eight dollars. Somebody's grandfather probably wore it to church. I took it to a tailor, spent forty on the alterations, and now it looks like it flew here first class." She smooths a lapel with something like affection. "That's the secret nobody wants to hear, because it's boring. *Tailoring.* It's not glamorous. There's no app for it. But it's the whole game."

---

## The Democracy of Looking Good

What strikes me, as we talk, is that Davis isn't peddling the usual influencer fantasy—the "you too can have this if you buy my seventeen affiliate links" hustle. Her philosophy is almost aggressively practical, and there's a populist streak to it that feels, in this particular economy, borderline radical.

"I grew up watching my mother do this," she says, quieter now. "She had one good coat and made it work for a decade. She could walk into any room and you'd think she summered somewhere. She didn't. She summered at the laundromat." A pause. "She taught me that presentation is the one luxury that's actually free. Well—" she gestures at herself, "—forty-eight dollars, in the case of this outfit."

I do the math on my own ensemble, which cost considerably more and, I'm now realizing, fits me considerably worse. It's a humbling afternoon.

"Don't do that," she says, catching my face. "Don't spiral. Everybody's first reaction to me is to feel bad about their clothes. That's the opposite of the point." She sets down her cup. "The point is *you can do this*. Anybody can. It's not a talent, it's a habit. Buy less. Fix what you have. Iron things—God, please, people, own an iron. And figure out what actually fits your body instead of what fits some mannequin."

---

## The Exit

As we wrap, a young woman approaches nervously, clutching a garment bag, asking for a photo. Davis lights up, throws an arm around her, and I catch her whispering something about the girl's jacket—a suggestion, a tiny tailoring tip, delivered like a state secret.

Then she's off, ivory blazer and all, cutting through the crowd like a woman who paid a fortune to look this way.

She didn't. That's the whole point. And as I gather my notes, I make a quiet vow to finally learn where my nearest tailor is.

Eight dollars. I still can't get over the eight dollars.
